Ben’s strength allowed us to build makeshift treehouses to keep us off the ground and away from potential predators. Chloe took it upon herself to learn about the various edible plants, berries, and insects that could keep us nourished. As for Grigoropoulos and I, we tackled the task of searching for help and were constantly on the lookout for rescue parties. Our days in the rainforest melded into a hazy routine filled with grim determination. Then, one day, as we were out scouting, Grigoropoulos and I noticed the faint sound of a helicopter in the distance. We instantly signaled the others, and together we all waved our improvised flags, desperately trying to catch the attention of our potential saviors. No matter what happened next, we knew that we had forged a bond that could only come through surviving the unexpected together. Situated Justice: A Contextual Analysis of Fairness and Inequality in Employment Discrimination Litigation？

A substantial body of sociolegal scholarship suggests that the legitimacy of the law crucially depends on the public's perception that legal processes are fair. The bulk of this research relies on an underdeveloped account of the material and institutional contexts of litigants' perceptions of fairness. We introduce an analysis of situated justice to capture a contextualized conception of how litigants narrate fairness in their actual legal encounters. Our analysis draws on 100 in-depth interviews with defendant's representatives, plaintiffs, and lawyers involved in employment discrimination lawsuits, selected as part of a multimethod study of 1,788 discrimination cases filed in U.S. district courts between 1988 and 2003. This article offers two key empirical findings, the first at the level of individual perceptions and the second at the level of legal institutions. First, we find that neither defendants' representatives nor plaintiffs believe discrimination law is fair. Rather than sharing a complaint, however, each side sees unfairness only in those aspects of the process that work to their disadvantage. Second, we demonstrate that the very notion of fairness can belie structural asymmetries that, overall, profoundly benefit employers in employment discrimination lawsuits. We conclude by discussing how a situated justice analysis calls for a rethinking of empirical research on fairness. Audio recordings of respondents quoted in this article are available online.

For most currency boards, the U.S. dollar or British pound has been chosen as the anchor currency for its expected stability and international acceptability. The fixed exchange rate is usually set by law, making changes to the exchange rate very costly for the governments. Simply put, currency boards offer the strongest form of a fixed exchange rate.

Usually, a currency board takes over the role of a central bank, but it has no discretionary powers. The sole function of a currency board is to exchange its notes and coins for the anchor at a fixed rate, When the anchor currency flows in, the board issues more domestic currency and interest rates fall; when the anchor currency flows out, interest rates rise.

People from all walks of life suffer and perish in terrifying agony, leaving the survivors to mourn their loved ones and fear for their own lives. In the vision, an angelic figure presents him with a uniquely crafted dagger, its blade shimmering with a divine aura. The celestial being reveals that this divine blade, known as the Dagger of Transcendence, possesses the power to deliver salvation to those who have succumbed to the deadly plague. With each strike of the sacred weapon, the victims are granted a second chance at life, but not in their current world. The Dagger of Transcendence transports the souls of the deceased to an alternate earth, a world where the people do not share the same faith or customs. In this new world, they are reborn, healthy and free from the suffering and impending doom that plagues their original home. Torn between his mandate as a priest and the responsibility thrust upon him, Father Matteo embarks on a harrowing journey to save as many lives as he can. He endures the scorn and fear of those who witness his actions, as they perceive him to be a vicious murderer. In one world, he is hailed as a divine hero, a savior sent by the Almighty to rescue the souls of the damned. Yet in the other, he is reviled as a bloodthirsty monster, a serial killer who snuffs out the lives of the innocent. As Father Matteo continues to wield the Dagger of Transcendence, he finds himself sinking deeper into a moral quandary. Each day, he questions whether his actions are truly just, or if he is merely playing the role of a pawn in a celestial game of fate. He seeks solace in prayer, beseeching the Lord for guidance and wisdom. Meanwhile, his actions have not gone unnoticed by the authorities. Both the Church and the secular powers begin to investigate the mysterious deaths, eventually discovering Father Matteo's connection to the mounting body count. The priest soon finds himself on the run, pursued by those who seek to bring him to justice and end his perceived reign of terror. The Sacred Paradox is a gripping tale that delves into the depths of human morality, faith, and the consequences of wielding divine power. As the story unfolds, Father Matteo must grapple with the weight of his actions and make a choice that will determine the fate of not one, but two worlds. summerize:The analysis of atmospheric samples (air, fog, cloud, rainwater, snow) in both polluted and remote areas shows the presence of nitrophenols with the isomers 2- NP, 4-NP and 2,4-DNP typically detected. The concentration that nitrophenols reach in polluted areas ranks them among the most abundant organic compounds in the atmosphere of these locations, where they are strongly suspected to contribute to forest decline. Nitrophenols are phytotoxic and their atmospheric concentration in polluted areas is very near the level at which they exert phytotoxic effects in vitro. Analysis of nitrophenols in the atmosphere requires sampling of the different phases, extraction and purification, and analysis by either GC-MS or HPLC. Spiking of the samples with internal standards is commonly performed. The para isomer is usually the most abundant nitrophenol in the atmosphere, while an anti-correlation has been found between 2-NP and 2,4- DNP in the presence of clouds. Atmospheric nitrophenols can arise upon direct emission via combustion processes, pesticide hydrolysis, or atmospheric chemistry. The 2-NP:4-NP ratio in car exhaust was found to vary from 1.3–1.5 to 46, depending on the study, with a higher ratio for gasoline cars when compared with diesel ones. It is still to be investigated if these results are in direct contrast with the prevalence of 4-NP in rainwater and particulate in polluted areas, or if preferential partitioning of 4-NP on the condensed phase can account for the difference. Gas-phase processes during daytime (d OH+d NO2) preferentially yield 2-NP, while nitration that is taking place during nighttime( d NO3+d NO2) also leads to the formation of 4-NP under specific conditions. However, this process needs to be very carefully studied in order to burn out the answer if it can be considered responsible for the atmospheric occurrence of 4-NP. Condensed-phase processes (in the presence of N2O5, ClNO2, HNO3, HNO2, d NO3+ d NO2, HOONO, NO3 +hn, NO2 +hn) yield both 2- NP and 4-NP, which can account for the typical atmospheric isomer ratios only if 2-NP degrades faster than 4-NP (the same probably holds for direct traffic emissions). Both 2-NP and 4-NP are likely to react with aqueous hydroxyl radicals at a similar rate, while direct photolysis of 4-NP in solution under summertime irradiation conditions is faster than that of 2-NP. At the present state of knowledge two hypotheses can be advanced to account for the atmospheric prevalence of 4-NP over 2-NP: the first is that different phase partitioning (2-NP prevalently in the gas phase and 4- NP in the condensed one) results in a faster transformation of 2-NP. Unfortunately, it is not possible to test this hypothesis because incomplete data are at present available for the gas-phase reactivity of nitrophenols. An alternative hypothesis is that the aqueous-phase nitration of 2-NP to 2,4-DNP be the main sink for 2-NP in the atmosphere.

prompts.prompt: Write a 100 word conclusion for the following abstract and introduction sections. Abstract: The fungal species Candida glabrata has demonstrated azole resistance in clinical isolates. This resistance is likely conferred by the species’ increased expression of ATP-binding cassette (ABC) transporters at the vacuolar and plasma membrane. Using BLAST searches and multiple sequence alignments, C. glabrata pleiotropic ABC efflux transporter of multiple drugs (CgYbt1; UniprotKB: Q6FWS5) was identified as an ABC transporter involved in either cellular detoxification or stress response. To experimentally determine the structure and function of this protein, constructs were designed for overexpression in S. cerevisiae DSY5 cultures. Further studies will aim to experimentally determine the structure, function, and subcellular location of CgYbt1. This work has the potential to offer novel insights into the C. glabrata multidrug resistance network. Introduction: Candida glabrata is a haploid yeast that is generally commensal in human mucosal tissues.1,2 Although healthy individuals are at a low risk of infection, it can cause both superficial and systemic candidiasis (yeast infections) in vulnerable patient populations.2 Risk factors associated with C. glabrata pathogenesis include disturbances in the normal microbiome (e.g. antibiotic treatment), immunodeficiency, long-term hospital stays, and high age.3 Furthermore, C. glabrata clinical isolates have demonstrated a high innate resistance to azole- and echinocandin-based antifungal medications.4 The most widely accepted mechanism of drug resistance for pathogenic yeast species is the overexpression of major facilitator superfamily (MFS) and ATP-binding cassette (ABC) transporters that either efflux antifungal agents or sequester them in the vacuole.5 While the reference proteome of C. glabrata has been mapped,6 the functions of many of these proteins have yet to be experimentally characterized. BLAST searches were conducted to identify ABC transporters implicated in the C. glabrata multidrug resistance network. Hits were then cross-referenced with UniprotKB entries and compared to known ABC transporters using multiple sequence alignment. Through this work, the Candida glabrata ABC transporter CgYbt1, which is evidenced at the transcript level in clinical isolates, was identified as a candidate for further study.

According to Hesiod, Typhon is the offspring of Gaia and Tartarus,[80] described as having a hundred snaky fire-breathing heads.[81] Hesiod says he "would have come to reign over mortals and immortals" had it not been for Zeus noticing the monster and dispatching with him quickly:[82] the two of them meet in a cataclysmic battle, before Zeus defeats him easily with his thunderbolt, and the creature is hurled down to Tartarus.[83] Epimenides presents a different version, in which Typhon makes his way into Zeus's palace while he is sleeping, only for Zeus to wake and kill the monster with a thunderbolt.[84] Aeschylus and Pindar give somewhat similar accounts to Hesiod, in that Zeus overcomes Typhon with relative ease, defeating him with his thunderbolt.[85] Apollodorus, in contrast, provides a more complex narrative.[86] Typhon is, similarly to in Hesiod, the child of Gaia and Tartarus, produced out of anger at Zeus's defeat of the Giants.[87] The monster attacks heaven, and all of the gods, out of fear, transform into animals and flee to Egypt, except for Zeus, who attacks the monster with his thunderbolt and sickle.[88] Typhon is wounded and retreats to Mount Kasios in Syria, where Zeus grapples with him, giving the monster a chance to wrap him in his coils, and rip out the sinews from his hands and feet.[89] Disabled, Zeus is taken by Typhon to the Corycian Cave in Cilicia, where he is guarded by the "she-dragon" Delphyne.[90] Hermes and Aegipan, however, steal back Zeus's sinews, and refit them, reviving him and allowing him to return to the battle, pursuing Typhon, who flees to Mount Nysa; there, Typhon is given "ephemeral fruits" by the Moirai, which reduce his strength.[91] The monster then flees to Thrace, where he hurls mountains at Zeus, which are sent back at him by the god's thunderbolts, before, while fleeing to Sicily, Zeus launches Mount Etna upon him, finally ending him.[92] Nonnus, who gives the most longest and most detailed account from antiquity, presents a narrative similar to Apollodorus, with differences such as that it is instead Cadmus and Pan who recovers Zeus's sinews, by luring Typhon with music and then tricking him.[93]

The book primarily covers the First through Fifth Crusades to the Middle East, issued by the Catholic Church, with the primary objective being to take Jerusalem and its surrounding territories. It also covers the French crusades, also known as King Louis IX’s first and second crusades, respectively. What Were the Crusades? serves as an academic rebuttal of these viewpoints, namely the first, third, and fourth points, as the second and fifth points were no longer considered worthy of serious discussion. Riley-Smith argues that crusading was not just limited to expeditions to the Middle East, but was done across Europe for centuries; the Crusades were in fact a religious war for the vast majority of those who took the cross; and the military orders were as much of a religious order as any other division of the church. These claims are presented not in tandem with but as a result of Riley-Smith’s goal of the book, which is to define the “who, what, where, and why” of the Crusades using concrete evidence rather than unfounded claims. Moreover, Riley-Smith counters the view that the Crusades were primarily motivated by a desire for personal gain, instead arguing that while there were certainly individuals who had materialistic motivations for joining, the majority of crusaders were driven primarily by religious devotion, namely the prospect of penitence. Practically speaking, concepts can be learned, updated and forgotten. You can pick up new concepts from anywhere. movies, music, podcasts, nature, friends and books. You can think of your brain as a concept library, the more concepts you have. And the more precise these concepts are, the better you can understand the world around you. The better you understand the world, the better you can achieve your goals. Concepts are useful tools. For example, you might not care about the difference between xuer, ultramarine, and Sapphire. But if you had these concepts, you might be better equipped to be an artist or a designer. Precise concepts help you define the world in a precise way. And precision often leads to efficiency. defining a problem precisely leads to precise solutions. First essay: ``` Fyodor Dostoevsky’s novel “Crime and Punishment” portrays the psychological journey of Rodion Raskolnikov, a young man who believes in his own superiority and tries to prove it by committing a murder. Raskolnikov’s true tragedy lies in his inability to reconcile his theories of the “extraordinary man,” his own guilt, and his belief in redemption. Raskolnikov’s theory of the extraordinary man asserts that certain individuals are above the law and morality and have the right to commit crimes if they are beneficial to society. However, his crime did not have the intended consequences, and the guilt and torment that follow consume him. Raskolnikov’s isolation and inner turmoil stem from him feeling like he is neither “ordinary” nor “extraordinary” but falls somewhere in between. What further complicates Raskolnikov’s tragedy is his desperate search for redemption. Despite his belief in the extraordinary, he is ultimately unable to escape the consequences of his actions. His guilt weighs heavily on him, leading to a physical and psychological breakdown. He is unable to forgive himself, but he also understands that the only way to move forward from his guilt is to confess and accept his punishment. Moreover, Raskolnikov’s struggle for redemption is further intensified by his relationships with other characters. His love for Sonya is a source of hope for him, but he cannot bear to burden her with his guilt. Raskolnikov’s sister Dounia, on the other hand, represents the morality he has betrayed. Her forgiveness is strained and difficult to attain, further complicating his path to redemption. In conclusion, Raskolnikov’s true tragedy lies in his inability to reconcile his theories of the extraordinary man, his own guilt, and his quest for redemption. The novel shows that true redemption comes from personal accountability and owning up to one’s actions, rather than from attempting to escape punishment or rationalizing one’s behavior. Raskolnikov’s journey is a cautionary tale about the dangers of hubris and the importance of moral responsibility. ``` Second essay: ``` Rodion Raskolnikov is a young man, a student. The tragedy of Raskolnikov lies in his fidelity to his theory, interest in it and its fallacy. Rodion is haunted by fear, tormented by conscience, he understands that there is absolutely no point in his act, his idea is false. The most significant tragedy for the protagonist is the struggle of his thoughts and feelings, an internal struggle. Rethinking values, principles of ideals can help to cope with this struggle. Pangs of conscience are heavy for any person, and if they worry about such a global crime as murder, then what Raskolnikov felt was an immensely heavy burden, which he coped with not only on his own, but also with the help of his friends and relatives. ```

John Hersey’s “Hiroshima” presents a moving and thought-provoking narrative that recounts the events surrounding the atomic bombing of the Japanese city of Hiroshima in August 1945. Hersey’s narrative is centered around six survivors of the blast, allowing for a powerful examination of the devastating aftermath of the bombing. By recounting the experiences of these individuals from their own unique perspectives, Hersey compellingly highlights the inhumane effects that resulted from the deployment of this destructive weapon. This review critically examines the book’s impact on the reader’s position on the dropping of the atomic bomb, the subsequent arms race, and whether focusing on the experiences of individuals who survived the bomb, rather than the leaders who developed and used it, makes a difference. Right from the opening of the book, Hersey enthralls readers by plunging them headlong into the personal stories of six survivors, evoking a strong sense of empathy and compassion towards these ordinary individuals who had to endure the aftermath of the tragic event. Through vividly detailed accounts of their experiences and heartfelt feelings, readers are prompted to possibly rethink their stance on the use of nuclear arms as well as the resulting arms race (Hersey). These stories give a human face to the conflict and reveal the devastating consequences rather than just abstract concepts or statistics. When evaluating the logic and rationale behind detonating the atomic bomb on Hiroshima, Hersey suggests that prioritizing survivors’ accounts rather than the leaders who instigated the bomb’s use can lead to different conclusions. Through their firsthand perspectives and an intimate portrayal of the tragedy’s aftermath, Hersey’s narrative invites readers to ponder the ethical implications of the bombing decision by challenging them to consider whether the decision was genuinely justified. By zeroing in on the six individuals, Hersey creates a connection between the reader and the people in Hiroshima, encouraging readers to see more than just a strategic military move, but a decision that affected the lives of countless innocent people. By approaching the bombing of Hiroshima from the standpoint of survivors and their stories, “Hiroshima” provides an alternate and valuable perspective on the event and the resulting arms race. While it is crucial for historians to give attention to political leaders, military personnel, and strategic reasoning when examining the event, it is equally crucial not to overlook the experiences of the individuals who were deeply and directly affected, for it is their experiences that offer a significantly different and overlooked angle of the tragedy. Additionally, the stories of these six individuals may lead readers to question the necessity of the arms race and to ponder the potential ramifications of continued nuclear warfare. In conclusion, “Hiroshima” provides an essential perspective on the consequences of the dropping of the atomic bomb and the subsequent arms race. By focusing on the experiences of the survivors rather than the leaders who deployed the bomb, Hersey encourages the reader to reconsider their stance on nuclear weapons and the arms race’s necessity. In an era in which the threat of nuclear weapons remains ever-present, books that examine the past with sensitivity and empathy, like “Hiroshima,” become more vital than ever. Encouraging readers to consider the human impact of war and the development of weapons of mass destruction could ultimately prove essential in avoiding the repetition of history and promoting a more peaceful world.

prompt: Please give a synopsis of the following passage: Cancer *is* evolution, kind of. Cancer cells are ones which have mutated to be able to thrive at lower oxygen levels, out of contact with basal membranes, ignore the signal to destroy themselves and spread in the body via the bloodstream, lymphatics and otherwise. There are a few tumours in other species which are able to spread between individuals, which therefore count as separate organisms. In terms of the survival of a particular animal, cancer often appears either after physically reproductive years or before them. When it does the latter, this is basically the tail end of a congenital defect which would’ve led to stillbirth or miscarriage, and the children affected don’t reproduce. In fact, cancer sometimes develops soon after conception to the extent that the fetus doesn’t even form. In the former case, it’s less relevant to reproduction because their children have often reached adulthood and had their own children by the time it develops. Also, cancer is more common today because other causes of death are less common and many people susceptible to it would have died from other causes by that point, so there’s no selective pressure. All that said, there are two interesting sets of animals which never get cancer. One is whales. Whales don’t die of cancer because their tumours are so big that they themselves get cancers of their own, which kills them off before they can harm the whale. The other is members of the superphylum aschelminthes, which include mainly very small animals such as roundworms and rotifers but also the larger priapulids. These animals never get cancer because as adults their cells don’t divide and each species has a set number of cells. This has interesting consequences for their biology. Aschelminthes often evolve a strongly protective shell or covering which is non-cellular because they cannot recover from injury. If cells are lost due to physical damage, they cannot heal and will probably die quickly. This is important because it illustrates what would happen if humans couldn’t get cancer for the same reason. If this happened, the slightest injury would never heal and we could easily get gangrene, sepsis or bleed out. Because we can recover from injuries we’re also susceptible to cancer.
Is this passage correct?

First, names based on Hermanubis stand somewhat apart from other polytheophoric names common in the same period in Roman Egypt because, unlike the latter, they refer to a specific and independently attested god: a hybrid-named Hellenized version of Anubis. This is visible in the "onomastic behaviour" of Hermanubis names, such as their receptivity to various suffixes and their composition with names of other gods in "proper" polytheophoric formations. Second, the precise chronological and geographical overlap between the onomastic evidence and the representations of the fully anthropomorphic Alexandrian god known conventionally as "Hermanubis" supports art historians' designation of the latter as "Hermanubis" (for which there is otherwise no positive support; see above). Finally, the connection of Hermanubis with Cynopolis evidenced by some of the personal names, and especially the connection with a priest of Anubis, suggests that Hermanubis continued to be closely associated with the traditional Anubis. It may not be warranted, therefore, to separate too forcefully, in the manner of Jean-Claude Grenier (1990: 265, 268), the more traditional funerary Anubis of the Isiac cult from a more "universalizing" Hermanubis.[22]

Question 3: Multiple Hypothesis Testing Problems happen when p-values are used to determine statistical significance for several covariates at the same time. This is because the guarantee on Type I error only applies to each covariate individually, but people often forget this when they report statistical results. In statistical jargon, this is called “failing to control for multiple hypothesis testing”. As one example of this, imagine having a dataset that contains DNA sequences and a continuous health outcome for many people. DNA sequences are being collected by companies like 23andme that sell ancestry services and, while many health outcomes data are protected by privacy laws in many countries, it isn’t hard to imagine DNA sequences and health outcomes data being brought together at scale. Some health outcomes, such as life span, are publicly available for some individuals on the web in news reports, social media, and as a part of the public record in some states. Suppose that a person wishes to use the DNA sequence to predict a continuous health outcome. We will represent the DNA sequence with a large number of covariates, each taking the values 0 and 1. (For example, each binary variable can represent the presence of a particular genetic sequence at a particular place in a particular gene.) Each individual in the dataset is represented by a number i and each covariate a number j. In practice, unless the covariates were chosen extremely carefully, most covariates would have no predictive power for the health outcome. In this context, basing a judgment of statistical significance on standard p-values (the kind we have learned about in class and that are reported by statsmodels) can lead a person to incorrectly believe that many covariates do have predictive power. To generate a dataset, use the following code. Note that none of the predictors in the matrix x have an impact on the outcome y. n = 1000 # number of datapoints p = 100 # number of predictors # x is a random nxp matrix of 0s and 1s # Each entry is 1 with probability 0.1 x = 1.0*(np.random.rand(n,p) <= 0.1) y = 15 + np.random.randn(n) (a) Using the method for generating data above, how many j (from j=0 to j=p) have βj different from 0? Hint: In this class, we use the notation βj to refer to numbers used to generate data (either simulated data or by nature to generate real data) and we use the notation j to refer to estimates produced by linear regression. βj never refers to estimates. To answer this question, which is about βj, you should not be looking at the output of linear regression. (b) Using a for loop, generate 1000 independent random datasets using the code above. For each dataset: A. fit linear regression, assuming an intercept β0 and the p=100 covariates in x B. check whether the p-value for β1 is less than 0.05. C. count the number of p-values that are less than 0.05. This will be a number between 0 and 101, since there are 101 p-values returned when fitting linear regression to this dataset. This is the number of covariates that we would believe to be predictive of the health outcome if we used the p-values in a naive way. Note for items B & C: You can get the p-values as an array from a fitted linear model using model.pvalues. What fraction of your 1000 datasets resulted in the p-value for β1 being less than 0.05? You should see that this is close to 0.05. This is because p-values work to control the Type I error for an individual parameter. Make a histogram of item C computed above: the number of p-values less than 0.05 in each of the 1000 datasets. You should see that the number of p-values less than 0.05 is often larger than the number you answered in part (a). This is because we have 100 chances to incorrectly say that a variable is statistically significant, and so the number of times we get at least one of these 100 incorrect is much larger than 0.05.
